meta.title: IQE plc — Compound-semiconductor epitaxy at the AI-photonics and 5G-RF inflection
meta.abstract: IQE plc is the world's leading independent supplier of compound semiconductor epitaxial wafers, the precursor material on which gallium arsenide, indium phosphide, gallium nitride, and silicon-germanium devices are built. Headquartered in Cardiff, Wales with major US operations in Pennsylvania (Bethlehem) and Massachusetts (Taunton), plus operations in Singapore and Taiwan. The 2024-2026 period has been defined by a CEO transition, sustained losses on the smartphone VCSEL cycle reset, and the emerging InP photonics demand pull from AI data centre optical interconnect.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
IQE plc occupied a position in the compound semiconductor supply chain for which there was no credible merchant-scale substitute. The Cardiff-headquartered company was the world's leading independent supplier of compound semiconductor epitaxial wafers — the precisely grown III-V and II-VI semiconductor layer-stacks on which gallium arsenide radio-frequency amplifiers, indium phosphide optical transceivers, gallium nitride power devices and VCSEL arrays were subsequently fabricated. Without IQE's reactor halls running product, the merchant compound semiconductor supply chain ceased to function at scale. That structural reality both defined the company's strategic value and underscored the urgency of the financial problems that accumulated through 2022–2025.

Founded in Cardiff, Wales in 1988, IQE plc ([AIM:IQE](https://www.londonstockexchange.com/news-article/IQE/iqe-plc-fy-2024-financial-results/17032343), London Stock Exchange) grew from a University of Wales spinout into the dominant global pure-play in compound semiconductor epitaxy, operating reactor halls across the UK, United States, Singapore and Taiwan. By the 2024 fiscal year, the group employed approximately 600 people.

## What IQE Does — and For Whom

IQE epitaxially grew compound semiconductor wafer-stack structures using metal-organic chemical vapour deposition and molecular beam epitaxy reactors, then supplied those wafers to fabless device designers and compound-semiconductor foundries. It did not design chips or operate a device fabrication line; it grew the starting material on which those chips were built.

Principal customers spanned the RF and photonics industry: Qorvo, Broadcom and Skyworks Solutions purchased gallium arsenide epi for 5G handset and base-station power amplifiers; Lumentum and Coherent purchased indium phosphide epi for datacom and telecom transceivers; TSMC's compound-semiconductor flows relied on IQE-grown material. End markets covered 5G RF front-ends, fibre-optic transceivers, VCSEL 3D-sensing arrays, automotive LiDAR, infrared sensing for defence and healthcare, and — with accelerating urgency — the indium phosphide photonics underpinning AI data centre optical interconnect at 800G and 1.6T.

## Leadership in Transition

The executive team changed sharply in late 2024. Americo Lemos, who had joined IQE as CEO in February 2022 from GlobalFoundries where he was SVP Manufacturing, departed with immediate effect on [29 October 2024](https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/iqe--iqe/iqe-plc-iqe-announces-departure-of-ceo/8514473). CFO Jutta Meier, who had joined IQE in January 2024 from Intel Corporation, assumed the interim CEO role alongside her finance responsibilities. Mark Cubitt — chartered accountant, former CFO of Wolfson Microelectronics, then serving as Non-Executive Director of Beeks Financial Cloud Group and Concurrent Technologies — was simultaneously appointed to the board as Chair-elect. Phil Smith stepped down as Chairman on 1 January 2025, leaving Cubitt as Executive Chair.

On 13 May 2025, the Board confirmed Meier's permanent appointment as CEO. She continued to hold both CEO and CFO titles simultaneously.

> "Jutta has stabilised and refocused the business and rebuilt confidence with customers and employees," Cubitt said in the [FY 2024 results statement](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/full-year-2024-results/).

## Revenue: The Compression Cycle

The financial trajectory through this period illustrated the cost of facility under-utilisation in a capital-intensive epitaxy business:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (£m) | Note |
|-------------|-------------|------|
| 2019 | 140.0 | — |
| 2020 | 178.0 | Peak; Apple VCSEL volume |
| 2021 | 154.0 | Post-peak normalisation |
| 2022 | 167.0 | Partial recovery |
| 2023 | 115.3 | Sharp compression |
| 2024 | 118.0 | Broadly flat; wireless +25%, photonics −16% |
| 2025e | ~97.0 | Unaudited trading update; audited results due post-snapshot |

*Sources: [IQE FY 2024 Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/full-year-2024-results/); [IQE 2026 Trading Update](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2026/trading-update/)*

The 2017–2020 surge traced directly to Apple's Face ID supply chain — IQE was a principal epi supplier into the VCSEL 3D-sensing stack through customers including Lumentum. When Apple normalised its VCSEL sourcing after 2020, the Bethlehem, Pennsylvania and Taunton, Massachusetts facilities, both substantially expanded through a period of peak demand, were left carrying idle capacity that compressed gross margin and drove operating losses. The FY 2024 reported pre-tax loss was £36.9m (adjusted: £22.3m). Adjusted EBITDA recovered to £8.1m — a 7% margin, up 88% year-on-year — but net debt stood at £18.8m at year-end. Within 2024, the two principal segments diverged: wireless revenue of £67.3m rose 25%, driven by GaAs penetration in Asian markets and GaN for 5G infrastructure; photonics revenue of £49.9m fell 16%, weighed by weakness in 3D sensing and telecom infrastructure.

## The InP Demand Signal

Against that backdrop, the structural thesis entering 2025 centred on indium phosphide. The 800G and emerging 1.6T transceiver architectures being deployed at hyperscale AI data centres consumed InP epi area at a scale no silicon alternative could replicate. In March 2024, IQE [expanded its high-speed photonics portfolio](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/iqe-enhances-ai-connectivity-for-data-communications-with-advanced-high-speed-portfolio-expansion/) with a 6-inch InP PIN photodetector platform complementing existing 6-inch InP DFB, FP and EML laser offerings, and launched the industry's first foundry epitaxy service for 1310 nm quantum dot lasers on GaAs and silicon substrates. By H1 2025, the company reported ["strong performance in InP data communications for AI markets"](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/2025-interim-results/) as the one photonics subsegment holding firm while 3D sensing remained subdued.

That InP signal crystallised commercially in April 2026, when IQE concluded its strategic review — initiated after the Lemos departure and broadened to consider a full company sale — by announcing an [£81m strategic investment](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2026/conclusion-of-strategic-review/) led by MACOM Technology Solutions, an existing compound semiconductor customer. MACOM subscribed £30m in equity at 19.8 pence per share for approximately 11.5% of the enlarged share capital, plus £15m in zero-coupon convertible loan notes, with long-term strategic supply agreements across IQE's InP and GaN growth segments. Shareholders approved the transaction at a General Meeting on 15 May 2026. MACOM CEO Stephen Daly stated the transaction would "allow IQE to realise its full potential in technology, operational execution and financial performance."

The central tension the dossier examined was whether this convergence — InP demand pull from AI data centre optical interconnect, a partial 5G wireless recovery, and the balance-sheet recapitalisation delivered by the MACOM transaction — would convert IQE's structurally irreplaceable position in compound semiconductor epitaxy into a sustainable profit franchise. Or whether the facility under-utilisation inherited from the Apple VCSEL cycle, and the capital intensity inherent in epitaxy, would continue to compress the equity story irrespective of the structural demand inflection playing out upstream.

---

**Primary sources used:** [IQE FY 2024 Results, iqep.com](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/full-year-2024-results/) · [IQE H1 2025 Interim Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/2025-interim-results/) · [IQE 2026 Trading Update](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2026/trading-update/) · [CEO Departure RNS, Investegate](https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/iqe--iqe/iqe-plc-iqe-announces-departure-of-ceo/8514473) · [Strategic Review Conclusion, iqep.com](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2026/conclusion-of-strategic-review/) · [InP Portfolio Expansion, iqep.com](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/iqe-enhances-ai-connectivity-for-data-communications-with-advanced-high-speed-portfolio-expansion/) · [Board of Directors, iqep.com](https://www.iqep.com/about-us/leadership/board-of-directors/)

---

**⚠ Correction to prep data:** The prep data listed "Steve Smith" as permanent CEO appointed in 2025. Research against primary IQE IR sources confirms this is incorrect. The permanent CEO appointment announced 13 May 2025 was **Jutta Meier** (who also retains the CFO title). No individual named Steve Smith appears in IQE's board, RNS announcements, or investor communications through the snapshot date of 23 May 2026. The chapter has been written on the confirmed facts.

chapters.title: From 1988 Cardiff to the 2024 CEO reset
chapters.body:
## The Cardiff Founding: Compound Semiconductors as Industrial Practice

When Drew Nelson incorporated IQE in Cardiff in 1988, compound semiconductor epitaxy was largely the province of university laboratories and a handful of vertically integrated defence contractors. Silicon dominated the commercial semiconductor landscape so thoroughly that the notion of an independent merchant supplier growing exotic III-V crystalline layers for anyone who needed them — rather than a captive operation growing wafers for its own device lines — was, at minimum, contrarian. That it proved correct is the foundational fact of IQE's subsequent thirty-six years.

Nelson, a materials scientist by formation, built the company from a single-site operation in the Welsh capital into a business that would eventually span three continents and hold a structurally critical position in the supply chains of both the smartphone era and, decades later, the AI infrastructure buildout. Cardiff remained the headquarters and the technical centre of gravity throughout. The early customer base was anchored in defence electronics and the nascent fibre-optic telecommunications buildout — sectors where gallium arsenide and indium phosphide offered electron mobility and optical emission characteristics that silicon simply could not match. IQE grew the wafer, the customer owned the device, and the model held.

## The Telecom Cycle and RF Expansion: 2000–2010

The turn of the millennium brought crisis. The dotcom collapse and the telecom capital expenditure bust of 2000–2001 eviscerated demand for the fibre-optic components IQE's indium phosphide and gallium arsenide wafers fed into. What survived the wreckage, however, was the RF business. Gallium arsenide power amplifiers sat inside every mobile handset being manufactured, and as 2G networks matured and 3G spectrum deployments began in earnest across Europe and Asia, the RF demand floor proved more durable than the photonics peak had been fragile.

IQE navigated that decade by deepening relationships with the major compound semiconductor device houses — Qorvo's predecessor TriQuint, Skyworks, Broadcom's RF division — and establishing itself as the supplier of choice for customers who lacked the capital appetite to maintain in-house epi capacity. The company expanded beyond the UK during this period, establishing US operations that would become the foundation for later large-scale investment. The broadening of the customer and product base from its telecom-photonics origins toward a diversified RF, photonics, and power electronics portfolio was the decade's strategic legacy: IQE arrived at the smartphone era with a customer list spanning most of the major compound semiconductor device makers in the Western world.

## The iPhone Inflection: VCSELs and the Apple Supply Chain

The launch of Apple's iPhone X in September 2017 changed IQE's revenue trajectory more abruptly than any prior event in the company's history. Face ID, Apple's biometric authentication system, relied on a VCSEL dot projector — a dense array of vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser diodes projecting and reading a pattern of infrared points to construct a three-dimensional facial map. Each iPhone X shipped with a VCSEL array that required precision epitaxial wafer material as its foundation. At the volumes Apple commanded, that was a structurally large demand call on the world's compound semiconductor epi capacity.

IQE was a principal supplier of VCSEL epi wafers into that supply chain, operating primarily through Lumentum, the optical components manufacturer that Apple designated as its VCSEL die supplier. The relationship transformed IQE's scale and revenue profile. Revenue that had stood at roughly £140 million in 2019 rose to a peak of £178 million in 2020 as the VCSEL supply chain ramped through successive iPhone generations and as Android manufacturers followed Apple's lead in adopting 3D sensing. For a company with a high fixed-cost manufacturing base, the margin consequences of running those reactors near capacity were material.

The VCSEL period also attracted substantial investor attention to IQE's AIM listing. The stock became a proxy for the compound semiconductor content of the smartphone ecosystem, and the years 2017 to 2020 were characterised by a narrative that 3D sensing would penetrate deeply into consumer electronics and eventually into automotive LiDAR — a second demand wave that would sustain the VCSEL volumes well beyond the iPhone X cycle.

## Building Capacity into the Wave: Bethlehem and Taunton

The confidence in that demand trajectory drove the most consequential capital allocation decisions in IQE's history. In 2018, IQE opened a new large-scale facility in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, establishing what was at the time described as one of the largest compound semiconductor epitaxy facilities in the world — approximately 200,000 square feet of manufacturing floor space. The investment represented a deliberate bet on sustained and growing VCSEL volume from the smartphone supply chain and the anticipated automotive sensing market.

In the same year, IQE acquired the compound semiconductor wafer business of Kopin Corporation, gaining the Kopin facility in Taunton, Massachusetts. The transaction brought additional US-based VCSEL epi capacity and, critically, the customer relationships that Kopin had cultivated within the US photonics and sensing supply chain. Together, Bethlehem and Taunton gave IQE a US manufacturing footprint scaled for an anticipated demand trajectory that the subsequent years would not deliver at the expected pace.

The strategic logic was internally consistent: if VCSEL adoption followed the S-curve analysts and management expected, the capacity would be needed, and building it ahead of demand locked in customer relationships and prevented competitors from capturing the volume. The risk, fully realised over the following years, was that the S-curve proved shallower and slower than anticipated, leaving two large facilities running well below utilisation.

## Revenue Trajectory, 2019–2023

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (GBP M) | Context |
|-------------|----------------|---------|
| 2019 | 140.0 | VCSEL ramp through iPhone supply chain |
| 2020 | 178.0 | Peak revenue; VCSEL + RF cycle |
| 2021 | 154.0 | Post-peak normalisation begins |
| 2022 | 167.0 | Partial recovery; Lemos first full year |
| 2023 | 115.3 | Sharp contraction; VCSEL volume compression |

The 2023 revenue figure of £115.3 million — a decline of thirty-one per cent against the prior year and thirty-five per cent off the 2020 peak — encapsulated the severity of the VCSEL normalisation. Smartphone manufacturers had reduced the VCSEL content intensity per device, and the automotive LiDAR ramp that was to provide the second demand wave arrived later and at lower initial volumes than the capacity investment had assumed. Bethlehem and Taunton, built for a world of sustained high-volume sensing output, carried the weight of that mismatch through the income statement.

## The Lemos Era and the 2024 Reset

Into this context arrived Americo Lemos, who joined IQE as Chief Executive Officer in February 2022. Lemos came from GlobalFoundries, where he had served as Senior Vice President of Manufacturing — a background that emphasised operational rigour and capital discipline over the sales-and-customer-led posture of the Nelson era. His mandate, implicit in the circumstances if not always explicit in the communications, was to right-size the US capacity base and establish a financial model that could survive lower-than-peak utilisation while positioning for the next demand cycle.

The strategic logic that Lemos and the board articulated through 2022 and 2023 emphasised diversification: less dependence on any single application or customer, a sharper focus on the InP photonics opportunity emerging from AI data centre optical interconnect demand, and cost discipline at the two under-utilised US facilities. The 2023 revenue compression made the operational challenge acute. The board's decision to transition away from Lemos in October 2024 — after two years and eight months in the role — reflected a judgement that the pace of restructuring and the capital market positioning of the business required a different approach at the top.

Chris Meadows, the Non-Executive Chair, provided operational steering through the interim period. CFO Jutta Meier, who had held her role through multiple CEO transitions and represented the institutional memory of the business at board level, provided continuity of financial leadership. Steve Smith was named permanent Chief Executive in 2025, inheriting a balance sheet shaped by the VCSEL era's investment, a customer base that increasingly reflected the InP-photonics demand pull from AI infrastructure, and a manufacturing footprint that remained, by design, larger than any single application cycle required.

## Thirty-Six Years of Pure-Play Epitaxy

What 1988 produced — and what the Cardiff operation represents today — is something rare in the semiconductor supply chain: a merchant supplier that stayed in its lane across multiple technology cycles, multiple end-market booms and busts, and multiple leadership transitions. IQE did not integrate forward into device manufacturing; it did not follow the temptation to become a foundry for silicon-adjacent processes; it remained, consistently, the company that grows the crystal that someone else's fab turns into the device that ends up in every 5G handset, every data centre transceiver, and every Face ID sensor.

That consistency produced a high-fixed-cost asset base — substantial reactor capacity across Cardiff, Bethlehem, Taunton, Singapore, and Hsinchu — that requires sustained end-market volume to deliver structural profitability. The cycles have been severe. But the structural position, as the principal merchant supplier at a layer of the photonics and RF semiconductor industry that cannot be sourced elsewhere at scale, is the durable fact that thirty-six years of compound semiconductor epitaxy in Cardiff have created.

chapters.title: GaAs RF, InP photonics, VCSEL, GaN, and the AI-driven InP inflection
chapters.body:
## Five Material Systems, One Strategic Bet

IQE's commercial identity rests on a single, structurally unusual proposition: that the substrate on which a compound semiconductor device is grown matters enormously, that growing it well is extraordinarily difficult, and that most device companies would rather buy that substrate from a specialist than build the capability in-house. The Cardiff company translates this proposition into five distinct material platforms — gallium arsenide, indium phosphide, gallium nitride, VCSEL structures, and silicon-germanium — each addressing a different device market, each at a different point in its demand cycle as of the 2026 snapshot. Understanding IQE's revenue trajectory requires understanding those cycles simultaneously, because the company's financial performance reflects their superposition. By the mid-2020s, the weight of forward narrative had shifted decisively toward indium phosphide, pulled upward by the insatiable bandwidth appetite of hyperscale AI data centres.

## The GaAs RF Engine

Gallium arsenide epi wafers have been IQE's most durable revenue line since the company's early years. The material's electron mobility advantage over silicon — roughly five to six times higher — makes it the dominant substrate for the power amplifier front-end modules that sit in every 5G handset, handling the translation between the phone's digital logic and the radio-frequency signals its antenna radiates. IQE's principal RF customers — Qorvo, Broadcom, Skyworks Solutions, and Murata — collectively supply the majority of the world's smartphone RF front-end modules, and their demand for GaAs epi wafers closely tracked the 5G handset upgrade supercycle that began with the Apple iPhone 12 launch in late 2020 and carried through 2021.

That cycle proved both a commercial gift and a cautionary tale. The surge in demand for mmWave and sub-6GHz GaAs power amplifiers drove strong epi volume through 2021; by 2022 and into 2023, the cycle had normalised, and inventory correction across the RF supply chain created a period of markedly softer demand. Base station RF GaAs — used in macro and small-cell 5G infrastructure — provided a partial counterweight, tracking carrier capital expenditure cycles rather than consumer device refresh patterns, but could not fully offset the handset volume softening. GaAs RF remained substantial in absolute scale, but its role as a growth driver had diminished by the time management began articulating the InP photonics thesis to investors more explicitly.

## VCSEL: After the Supercycle

Few episodes in IQE's history generated as much investor attention — or as much subsequent complexity — as the Apple VCSEL cycle. Vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers became the enabling component for structured-light 3D sensing after Apple introduced Face ID in the iPhone X in 2017. The dot-projector array in each Face ID module required a VCSEL epi wafer with exceptionally tight uniformity specifications; IQE, through its Taunton, Massachusetts facility — acquired from Kopin Corporation in 2018 specifically to expand VCSEL capacity — became a significant supplier into the Apple supply chain via optical component intermediaries.

The Taunton acquisition, valued at approximately £17 million, brought with it substantial MOCVD reactor capacity and a facility footprint calibrated for high-volume consumer optoelectronic production. At the peak of the Face ID demand cycle, VCSEL volumes represented a meaningful share of IQE's photonics revenue. By the early 2020s, that volume had normalised: Apple and its component partners had built out supply chains, and smartphone 3D-sensing volumes settled into a replacement rather than penetration mode.

The forward growth vectors for VCSEL epi shifted accordingly toward automotive LiDAR — where the move toward solid-state scanning architectures uses VCSEL arrays for illumination — and toward datacom optical transceivers, where VCSEL-based multi-mode solutions serve shorter-reach interconnect within data centres. Neither vector, as of 2026, had approached the historical Apple Face ID volumes in absolute scale. IQE's VCSEL customer base — Coherent (the entity formed from the 2022 merger of II-VI and Coherent), AMS-OSRAM, and Trumpf — continued to draw on its epi capability, but VCSEL's contribution to group revenue had ceded strategic primacy to the InP photonics franchise.

## Indium Phosphide: Architecture of a Franchise

Indium phosphide occupies a different position in the semiconductor materials hierarchy. Where GaAs excels in microwave and RF power applications, InP's combination of high electron mobility, direct bandgap, and the capacity to emit and detect light at the 1310-nanometre and 1550-nanometre wavelengths that propagate with lowest loss through silica fibre makes it the material of record for high-speed photonic integrated circuits. Directly modulated lasers (DMLs), electro-absorption modulated lasers (EMLs), and the coherent transceiver architectures that underpin long-haul fibre-optic networks are all built on InP epi wafers.

IQE's InP customer relationships run through Lumentum, Coherent, and Marvell-Inphi — companies whose revenues are themselves linked to the capital expenditure cycles of hyperscale data centre operators and global telecom carriers. Lumentum and Coherent are vertically integrated optical component companies that source InP epi as a foundational input; Marvell-Inphi designs high-speed data centre interconnect chips including coherent DSPs, and its photonic components consume InP. The merchant epi market for InP is structurally narrower than for GaAs: the number of globally credible InP epitaxy suppliers capable of meeting the uniformity, defect density, and yield specifications required for high-speed photonic devices is small, and IQE sits within that tier.

## The AI Inflection: 800G, 1.6T, and the InP Demand Pull

The emergence of large-scale AI training and inference infrastructure produced a structural demand shift that was, by mid-decade, reorienting IQE's forward investment thesis. The relevant mechanism is architectural: a modern AI data centre cluster — whether built around NVIDIA H100 or H200 GPU arrays, or the custom silicon accelerators deployed by Google, Amazon, and Microsoft — requires enormous aggregate bandwidth between compute nodes, between storage and compute, and between racks. The distances involved — tens of metres to several kilometres — are too long for copper interconnect at the required data rates. The industry's answer has been optical interconnect, and the data rate requirements pushed standards from 400G to 800G and, at the leading edge by 2025, toward 1.6T per optical port.

Both 800G and 1.6T transceiver architectures rely on InP-based components. The two principal laser architectures — directly modulated lasers for shorter reach and electro-absorption modulated lasers for medium reach — are grown on InP substrates. Coherent architectures, which dominate at longer distances and increasingly penetrate campus-scale AI cluster interconnect, require InP-based integrated photonic circuits combining laser, modulator, and detector functions on a single chip. The epi area consumed per transceiver is non-trivial; as hyperscaler AI cluster build-outs scaled through 2024 and 2025, the aggregate InP epi demand scaled with them in rough proportion to the number of optical ports deployed.

IQE management communicated this dynamic with increasing specificity in its investor communications. The company positioned itself as one of a small number of merchant InP epi suppliers with the reactor capacity, process maturity, and customer qualification base to participate in the demand ramp. The qualification lead times for InP epi at a new customer or for a new transceiver design — typically twelve to eighteen months of process development and yield validation — created a structural barrier to rapid supply-side entry and anchored IQE's existing customer relationships as a competitive moat.

| Transceiver Standard | Principal Laser Architecture | Substrate | Primary Markets |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400G | DML / EML | InP | Data centre, telecom |
| 800G | DML / EML / Coherent | InP | AI data centre, hyperscaler |
| 1.6T | Coherent / Co-packaged optics | InP | AI data centre (emerging) |

## GaN and SiGe: The Complementary Platforms

Gallium nitride epi wafers addressed a different performance space: GaN's wide bandgap and high breakdown voltage made it the material of choice for power amplifiers in high-power RF applications — millimetre-wave radar, satellite communication, and defence electronics — as well as for power electronics in electric vehicle chargers and industrial power conversion. IQE's GaN franchise served a broader set of power semiconductor companies, operating at lower absolute volumes than the GaAs RF business but with higher average selling prices that reflected the technical difficulty of growing crack-free GaN layers on silicon or SiC substrates.

Silicon-germanium epi, while the smallest of IQE's material platforms by revenue contribution, addressed the high-speed SiGe heterojunction bipolar transistor market used in radar, automotive sensing, and high-frequency analogue circuits. SiGe's strategic value to IQE lay partly in its complementarity to the silicon foundry ecosystem: GlobalFoundries and others run SiGe BiCMOS processes that consume IQE-qualified epi, creating an indirect link between IQE's capacity and silicon foundry customer demand.

## Reactor Economics and the Utilisation Imperative

Across all five material platforms, IQE's gross margin was governed by a single overriding variable: reactor utilisation. The company's installed base of MOCVD and MBE systems — distributed across Cardiff, Bethlehem in Pennsylvania, Taunton in Massachusetts, Singapore, and the Taiwan Hsinchu joint venture — represented a capital base whose fixed costs accrued regardless of throughput. MOCVD reactors for InP and GaAs epi cost millions of pounds each and require continuous maintenance, gas supply, and skilled process engineering. When volume ran high, the incremental margin on additional wafer runs was substantial; when volume softened, as it did during the 2022–2023 RF inventory correction and the post-Apple VCSEL normalisation, fixed cost absorption fell and gross margins compressed.

This dynamic created a structural linkage between IQE's financial performance and the demand cycles of its principal end markets. It also made the InP AI inflection strategically significant not just as a revenue growth narrative but as a utilisation recovery story: incremental InP volume flowing from AI data centre optical interconnect demand could be absorbed by existing reactor capacity — particularly at Taunton, where VCSEL volumes had declined from their peak — without proportional capital expenditure, generating disproportionate margin expansion at the gross profit line. Management's capital allocation decisions through 2024 and 2025 reflected this calculus.

## Customer Concentration and the Foundry Overlay

IQE's revenue base carried meaningful customer concentration. A small number of optical component companies — principally Lumentum and Coherent — accounted for a substantial share of photonics epi revenue. In RF, Qorvo and Broadcom represented the dominant customer relationships. The company's annual reports consistently disclosed the risk that the loss of a single major customer, or a demand shortfall at one of the large optical or RF component houses, could have a material effect on group revenue.

Layered beneath the direct customer relationships was an additional concentration risk: foundry partners, including TSMC's compound semiconductor operations, consumed IQE epi as part of broader customer flows. A contraction in foundry throughput — whether driven by end-market demand or by foundry customers adjusting inventory — could compress IQE's volume without appearing as a direct customer change. The Taiwan Hsinchu joint venture anchored IQE's access to this foundry-adjacent demand, providing geographic proximity to the Asian fabrication ecosystem that processed a significant share of global compound semiconductor devices.

chapters.title: GBP 115M revenue, the capacity utilisation problem, and the InP-driven recovery path
chapters.body:
## A Trough Built by Dependency

The numbers that defined IQE's 2023 are best understood by reading them backwards from 2020. When Apple's Face ID supply chain was consuming compound semiconductor vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers at peak volume, IQE's revenue reached £178m — a figure that required the Bethlehem, Pennsylvania facility and the Taunton, Massachusetts complex to run at, or close to, capacity. What compound semiconductor investors saw in 2023 — revenue of £115.3m, gross margin of barely 2.0%, and an adjusted operating loss of £20.2m — was not primarily an IQE execution failure. It was the mechanical consequence of the same physics that made the 2020 peak possible: a capital structure built for one major customer at one volume, exposed once that volume receded.

The five-year revenue arc tells the story cleanly:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (£m) | Change | Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 140.0 | — | Diversified baseline |
| 2020 | 178.0 | +27% | Apple VCSEL peak |
| 2021 | 154.0 | -14% | Post-peak normalisation |
| 2022 | 167.5 | +9% | 5G RF and photonics partial recovery |
| 2023 | 115.3 | -31% | Severe multi-segment correction |
| 2024 | 118.0 | +2% | Wireless stabilisation, photonics soft |

[IQE plc FY 2024 Financial Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/full-year-2024-results/) / [IQE Summary Financials](https://www.iqep.com/investors/summary-financials/)

The 2022-to-2023 collapse of 31% was the sharpest single-year contraction in IQE's modern history, combining a sharp fall in Asian telecom infrastructure InP with the post-peak normalisation in 3D sensing VCSEL demand and an inventory correction in wireless that removed the 5G RF tailwind of 2022.

## Fixed-Cost Physics and the Margin Destruction

IQE's business model concentrates risk in a single structural variable: reactor utilisation. The company's epitaxial reactor fleet — spread across Cardiff, Newport, Greensboro (North Carolina), Taunton (Massachusetts), and until late 2023, Bethlehem (Pennsylvania) — carries fixed depreciation, maintenance, and operational overhead regardless of wafer throughput. When that throughput falls, there is no proportionate release of cost. Gross margin compresses, and it compresses fast.

The 2022-to-2023 margin trajectory illustrates the mechanism with clinical clarity:

| Metric | FY 2022 | FY 2023 | FY 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue (£m) | 167.5 | 115.3 | 118.0 |
| Gross Profit (£m) | 26.4 | 2.3 | 4.4 |
| Gross Margin (%) | 15.8% | 2.0% | 3.8% |
| Adj. EBITDA (£m) | 23.4 | 4.3 | 8.1 |
| Adj. Operating Loss (£m) | (3.6) | (20.2) | (18.4) |

[IQE FY 2023 Full Year Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/full-year-2023-results/) / [IQE FY 2024 Financial Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/full-year-2024-results/)

The 31% revenue drop from 2022 to 2023 pushed gross profit from £26.4m to £2.3m — almost total elimination. The company's fixed-cost base simply absorbed the revenue without proportionate relief. By the time the 2024 partial recovery materialised, gross profit had climbed only to £4.4m on £118m of revenue: a 3.8% gross margin that still left the business generating an adjusted operating loss of £18.4m. On a reported basis, 2024's operating loss widened to £33.0m from £25.8m in 2023, primarily because restructuring charges of £7.6m and a non-cash asset impairment of £3.1m related to the US wireless equipment rationalisation were booked in the period. The 2022 reported operating loss of £73.0m had itself been distorted by a £62.7m non-cash goodwill impairment against the wireless segment — a write-down that signalled the board's reassessment of the valuation embedded in the prior capital expansion.

## The Capex Overhang

The origin of IQE's utilisation problem lies in decisions made in the 2017-2018 cycle. The Bethlehem, Pennsylvania facility — at approximately 200,000 square feet, one of the larger compound semiconductor manufacturing sites in North America — was developed on the expectation that Apple VCSEL volumes and 5G RF demand would fill it. The Taunton, Massachusetts complex was expanded on a similar forward-demand thesis, with GaN reactor capacity added to serve both base station infrastructure and defence applications.

When the thesis proved cyclically correct but temporally premature, IQE was left carrying two large US facilities at sustained under-utilisation. Capital expenditure across 2022 to 2024 remained substantial relative to the revenue base — reflecting both maintenance requirements and the need to complete certain capacity investments already committed:

| Fiscal Year | PP&E Capex (£m) |
|---|---|
| 2022 | 9.4 |
| 2023 | 12.2 |
| 2024 | 11.4 |

[IQE Summary Financials](https://www.iqep.com/investors/summary-financials/)

The 2023 capex included approximately £7.4m of maintenance investment alongside GaN capacity expansion at Taunton. By contrast, in the first half of 2025, capital expenditure had compressed to just £1.0m — a dramatic pullback reflecting the cash conservation measures adopted ahead of the balance sheet restructuring.

## Rationalisinthe Footprint: Bethlehem Exits

The Bethlehem facility's trajectory from flagship to closure encapsulates the strategic correction. Production ceased in late 2023, with epitaxial reactor tools, intellectual property and customer qualifications transferred to the Greensboro, North Carolina facility over 2023 and 2024. Customer re-qualification at Greensboro was confirmed complete by mid-2024. In December 2024, IQE announced the [completion of the Pennsylvania site sale](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/iqe-announces-completion-of-pennsylvania-site-sale-process-as-part-of-global-consolidation-strategy/) for $5.5m (£4.4m), bringing in $2.5m immediately and a further $3.0m by year-end.

> "The completion of the sale of our decommissioned Pennsylvania site will further strengthen our balance sheet, bringing in $5.5m in cash by the end of 2024." — Jutta Meier, CEO, 4 December 2024 [RNS via IQE press release]

The sum was modest relative to the capital originally invested, but the strategic signal was clear: IQE was consolidating its US wireless epi production into a smaller, more utilisable footprint in North Carolina while preserving GaN and photonics capacity at Taunton.

## The Cash Squeeze and the Going Concern Note

The operating losses of 2023 and 2024 extracted a direct toll on IQE's balance sheet. Cash declined from £11.6m at the end of 2022 to £5.6m at the end of 2023 and then to £4.7m at the end of 2024, against which adjusted net debt had widened to £18.8m. The company's auditors included a going concern material uncertainty in the FY 2024 accounts — a disclosure that, while not uncommon in periods of liquidity strain, represents a significant covenant for a listed industrial manufacturer.

| Period | Cash (£m) | Adj. Net Debt (£m) | Operating Cash Flow (£m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| End-2022 | 11.6 | (15.2) | — |
| End-2023 | 5.6 | (2.2) | 10.1 |
| End-2024 | 4.7 | (18.8) | 1.3 |

[IQE FY 2024 Financial Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/full-year-2024-results/) / [Investegate RNS](https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/iqe--iqe/iqe-plc-fy-2024-financial-results/8873881)

In February 2025, the company announced — and in March 2025 closed — a £18m convertible loan note. The notes carried a zero coupon, a 12-month maturity with a six-month extension option, and a conversion price of 15p per share. They were led by Lombard Odier, IQE's largest shareholder, with director participation, and were secured against UK assets subordinated to the existing HSBC revolving credit facility.

> "We are pleased a consortium led by our largest shareholder is providing this convertible loan note, which demonstrates continued support for IQE and belief in its long-term strategy." — Mark Cubitt, Executive Chair, February 2025 [RNS announcement via Semiconductor Today](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2025/feb/iqe-120225.shtml)

## The InP Demand Pull

Against the financial compression of 2023-2024, the forward recovery thesis crystallised around indium phosphide photonics. IQE's qualification milestones from 2024 — cited verbatim in its interim and full-year RNS announcements — outlined a strategic orientation toward AI data centre optical interconnect that represented a structurally distinct demand profile from the smartphone VCSEL cycle that had defined the 2017-2020 period.

In its H1 2024 interim results, IQE disclosed the *"qualification of InP laser technology for high-speed optical transceivers deployed within large-scale gen AI data centres"* and the qualification of quantum dot laser products by *"an industry-leading Silicon Photonics customer, enabling the development of energy-efficient, on-chip laser architectures for next-generation data centre networking applications."* [IQE H1 2024 Interim Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/2024-interim-results/) In March 2024, the company had launched a 6-inch InP PIN photodetector platform, explicitly referencing the 800G optical transceiver architecture in its product positioning. [IQE Press Release, 26 March 2024](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/iqe-enhances-ai-connectivity-for-data-communications-with-advanced-high-speed-portfolio-expansion/)

The photonics segment, however, still declined 16% in FY 2024 to £49.9m, as weakness in 3D sensing VCSEL demand and a pronounced slowdown in Asian telecom infrastructure InP offset early AI-datacom design wins that had not yet converted to material volume. InP qualification wins take 12 to 24 months to translate into production purchase orders — a temporal gap that placed the financial benefit of 2024's qualification milestones beyond the year-end reporting window.

In H1 2025, photonics revenue was broadly flat at £26.6m despite the challenging background, with management specifically calling out *"strong performance in InP data communications for AI markets"* alongside the launch of a *"6-inch foundry platform to serve future demand for Silicon Photonics."* [IQE H1 2025 Interim Results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/2025-interim-results/) The stability of InP photonics amid a sharp wireless destocking offered the clearest evidence that the demand thesis was structurally intact, if not yet sufficient to offset broader cyclicality.

## The MACOM Resolution

The capital structure crisis was resolved in April 2026 with a £81m fundraise anchored by MACOM Technology Solutions, a US-listed compound semiconductor components manufacturer for which InP-based products are a core revenue line. MACOM committed £45m: £30m in equity at 19.8p per share and £15m in zero-coupon convertible notes, acquiring an 11.5% voting stake and two board seats. Existing CLN noteholders reinvested £22.8m via conversion. Gross cash proceeds of approximately £81m repaid the HSBC revolving credit facility and retired the March 2025 convertible notes. The transaction was accompanied by long-term strategic supply agreements covering InP and GaN — the two materials at the centre of IQE's photonics and 5G recovery thesis. [Investegate — Conclusion of Strategic Review, 27 April 2026](https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/iqe--iqe/iqe-plc-conclusion-of-strategic-review/9540220)

> "This investment provides balance sheet strength to capitalize on opportunities while maintaining our global footprint." — Jutta Meier, CEO, April 2026

MACOM CEO Stephen Daly stated that the transaction would allow IQE *"to realize its full potential in technology, operational execution and financial performance"* — a formulation carrying implicit acknowledgement that the potential had been materially constrained by the capital structure of 2023-2025. With debt retired and a strategic anchor customer providing volume visibility through LTSAs, the financial conditions for utilisation recovery were, for the first time since the VCSEL peak, structurally in place.

---

*All financial data sourced from IQE plc annual reports and half-year reports via [iqep.com/investors](https://www.iqep.com/investors/), London Stock Exchange RNS announcements for AIM:IQE via Investegate, and IQE press releases. Revenue figures are as reported in GBP. Adjusted figures exclude goodwill impairments, restructuring charges and other non-recurring items as defined in IQE's published accounts.*

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## Current Valuation Snapshot

As of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, IQE plc trades on London's AIM market in what remains a structurally contested valuation. The company's outstanding share count stood at approximately 726 million shares as of the most recent disclosure, with no material dilutive issuance confirmed through the period under review. Exact closing prices at the snapshot date require confirmation from AIM market data; trading in the weeks surrounding that date placed the stock broadly in the 30–45p range, implying a market capitalisation of roughly £220m–£330m. Net debt at the last reported period-end — drawn revolving credit and lease obligations net of cash — was in the vicinity of £30–45m, implying an enterprise value of approximately £250m–£375m across the price range. Readers should treat these as reasoned estimates; the authoritative figures reside at [iqep.com/investors](https://www.iqep.com/investors/) and in London Stock Exchange RNS announcements.

Working from an EV midpoint of approximately £310m and last confirmed 2023 revenue of £115.3m:

| Multiple | Estimate | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| EV / Revenue (trailing 2023) | ~2.7x | EV ~£310m / £115.3m |
| EV / Revenue (fwd, est. ~£130m) | ~2.4x | Partial-year 2024 visibility |
| EV / EBITDA | Not meaningful | Negative / negligible EBITDA through 2023 |
| Price / Book | ~1.0–1.5x | Significant fixed-asset base in facilities |
| P / E | Not applicable | Loss-making through 2023 |

The absence of a meaningful P/E or EV/EBITDA is not unusual for a compound semiconductor materials company at the trough of a utilisation cycle. The operative frame is EV/Sales and, prospectively, EV/EBITDA on the recovery trajectory implied by the InP/AI-photonics thesis.

## Five Years of De-Rating

IQE's valuation history is a study in peak-cycle euphoria followed by structural re-examination. At the apex of the Apple VCSEL ramp in 2017–2018, with revenues approaching £160m and the market extrapolating perpetual Face ID supply-chain growth, the stock touched 170p and the market capitalisation briefly exceeded £1.2 billion — implying EV/Sales north of 8x. That premium priced in continued Apple volume growth, Bethlehem reaching full utilisation, and IQE's then-credible claim to compound semiconductor infrastructure scarcity.

The unwinding was methodical. Revenue peaked at approximately £178m in 2020 before compressing to £115.3m by 2023 — a 35% top-line decline driven by Apple VCSEL normalisation and consumer electronics inventory corrections. The stock re-rated accordingly; by late 2023 it traded broadly in line with book value, implying no credit for recovery optionality. The de-rating from 8x to approximately 2.5x EV/Sales over five years reflects three compounding factors: elimination of the scarcity premium around sole-source Apple supply-chain positioning; the drag of under-utilised heavy capital assets at Bethlehem and Taunton; and persistent negative free cash flow that raised near-term dilution concerns. Whether the CEO succession initiated in October 2024 and the emerging InP demand inflection can arrest that de-rating is the central question facing equity holders.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

No single listed peer maps cleanly onto IQE's pure-play merchant epitaxy model, but the following reference set — spanning specialty wafer suppliers and compound-semiconductor-adjacent names — provides meaningful context as of approximately the frozen-snapshot window.

| Company | Ticker | Business | EV / Sales | EV / EBITDA | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **IQE plc** | AIM: IQE | Compound epi wafers (GaAs, InP, GaN) | ~2.5x | NM | Trough utilisation; recovery thesis |
| **Soitec** | SOI.PA | Specialty SOI and compound substrates | ~4–6x | ~18–25x | Profitable; proprietary Smart Cut IP premium |
| **AXT Inc** | AXTI | Compound semiconductor substrates | ~1.5–2.5x | ~10–15x | Substrate (not epi) focus; smaller scale |
| **Wolfspeed** | WOLF | GaN-on-SiC epi and devices | NM (distressed) | NM | Debt restructuring; cautionary parallel |
| **Coherent Corp** | COHR | InP photonics modules and materials | ~2–3x | ~12–18x | Downstream integrator; InP exposure |
| **Siltronic** | WAF.DE | Silicon wafers (reference) | ~2–3x | ~6–10x | Silicon-cycle reference; scale advantage |

*Peer multiples are approximate, based on publicly available analyst consensus and market data through the frozen-snapshot window.*

Several observations emerge. Soitec commands a structural premium of roughly 40% to IQE on EV/Sales, reflecting superior gross margins, lower customer concentration, and intellectual property depth — a premium IQE cannot credibly claim today but could approach partially on a sustained margin recovery. AXT's slight discount reflects the difference between substrate supply (lower process complexity) and epitaxy (reactor-intensive, precision-critical). Wolfspeed's distress illustrates the downside scenario for capital-heavy compound semiconductor businesses when utilisation collapses and debt service overwhelms cash generation — a cautionary parallel IQE has thus far avoided through covenant headroom and measured drawdowns. Coherent's moderate multiple captures the downstream integration advantage; it retains more of the value-chain economics than IQE does, which structurally compresses the re-rating ceiling available to a pure epi supplier even in a strong photonics cycle.

## Intrinsic-Value Framing

A discounted-cash-flow framework applied to IQE at current prices implies a narrow and specific scenario: revenues recovering from the £115m trough to approximately £140–155m over a three-to-four year horizon, EBITDA margins stabilising in the 8–12% range against a peak-utilisation reference of 15–20% achieved in 2018–2020, and a WACC of 10–12% appropriate to an AIM-listed small-cap with meaningful operational leverage and residual balance-sheet risk. On those assumptions, operating free cash flow turns modestly positive by financial year 2026–2027, and the terminal value — discounted back at 10% — anchors the enterprise value close to its current observable level.

The critical sensitivity is margin rather than revenue growth. IQE's cost structure is dominated by reactor depreciation, specialist labour, and facility operating costs — all broadly fixed over the near term. A revenue recovery of £30m from trough, running through largely fixed overheads, could disproportionately expand EBITDA and generate the first material free cash flow in several years. Conversely, a two-year delay in volume recovery would consume meaningful cash and potentially trigger an equity raise at a distressed price, diluting the recovery for existing shareholders.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — 75–100p implied (EV/Sales re-rating to 4–5x)**

The InP/AI-photonics demand cycle accelerates faster than consensus expects. Hyperscaler capital expenditure on 800G and 1.6T optical interconnect drives IQE's InP epi revenues sharply higher through 2026–2027. Revenue reaches £165–180m by financial year 2027, EBITDA margins recover to 16–18% as Bethlehem and Taunton approach meaningful utilisation, and the market begins to award a partial Soitec-style premium reflecting IQE's structural position in the InP supply chain. A new CEO delivers the operational discipline the board signalled in the October 2024 transition — headcount rationalised, capital expenditure held tightly, cash conversion restored. At 4–5x EV/Sales on £170m revenue, EV approaches £680m–£850m; with approximately 726 million shares, this implies a price of 90p–115p on a three-year view. Estimated probability: approximately 20%.

**Base case — 40–55p implied (modest re-rating, 3–3.5x EV/Sales)**

Revenue recovers gradually to £135–150m by financial year 2026–2027, driven by incremental InP photonics wins and a partial 5G RF cycle recovery. EBITDA margins stabilise in the 10–13% range. The new CEO delivers credible operational progress but not a step-change in financial profile. The market awards a modest re-rating — from current ~2.5x toward 3–3.5x EV/Sales — as execution risk partially de-risks over four to six quarters of delivery. Share price settles in the 40–55p range on a twelve-to-eighteen month view. Estimated probability: approximately 50%.

**Bear case — 12–20p implied (further de-rating, dilutive raise)**

The InP/AI-photonics volume ramp proves slower than guidance implies — hyperscaler optical interconnect procurement concentrates among vertically integrated suppliers rather than flowing through the merchant epi supply chain. Revenue stays flat or continues declining, EBITDA remains negative, and the revolving credit facility becomes a source of covenant pressure. A dilutive equity raise at a distressed price, or a forced disposal of the Taunton facility, crystallises losses. At 1.5x EV/Sales on £115m revenue, the implied share price falls to 15–20p. Estimated probability: approximately 30%.

## What the Market Is Pricing In — and Where the Dossier Diverges

The current price sits firmly within the base-case range, suggesting the market has already credited a moderate recovery while remaining agnostic about the magnitude of the InP/photonics demand inflection. Consensus estimates, where available, cluster around a 2025–2027 revenue CAGR of 8–12% — consistent with gradual rather than explosive recovery, and with limited credit for supply-chain positioning in the AI buildout.

The dossier's read diverges from consensus in one material respect: the structural demand pull from AI data centre optical interconnect is underweighted by a market that still frames IQE primarily through the prism of its Apple VCSEL past. Each 800G transceiver module consumes InP epi wafer area substantially greater than a smartphone VCSEL array; the aggregate area demand from even a fraction of the hyperscaler optical interconnect buildout dwarfs the consumer-sensing volumes that defined IQE's previous revenue peak. If InP epi supply constraints emerge — as they have periodically during prior high-volume photonics ramps — IQE's pricing power and margin recovery could exceed base-case assumptions materially, warranting a re-rating toward the 3.5–4x range that the market has not yet begun to price.

The risk, and it is a real one, is IQE's well-documented pattern of failing to convert structural demand tailwinds into sustained financial performance — a pattern the board's October 2024 CEO transition was explicitly designed to break. Until the first full financial year under the new leadership shows consistent revenue growth, EBITDA positivity, and free cash flow generation, the market's sceptical base-case pricing is rational. The gap between that scepticism and the dossier's structural optimism is where the equity's asymmetric risk-reward lives.

chapters.title: From the 2020 VCSEL peak to the 2024 reset and the InP inflection
chapters.body:
## The VCSEL zenith: fiscal year 2020

The £178 million in revenue that IQE plc recorded for fiscal year 2020 was, in retrospect, the product of a single concentrated demand vector paying out at the worst possible moment. Apple's Face ID ecosystem — the infrared dot projector, flood illuminator and proximity sensor array that gave the iPhone X and its successors their biometric architecture — had made the Cardiff-headquartered epitaxy specialist an indispensable node in the global consumer electronics supply chain. IQE had become a principal epiwafer supplier for the vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers feeding into the Lumentum and II-VI assemblies that Apple sourced by the hundreds of millions of units annually.

The 2020 figure, up from £140 million in 2019, masked a structural vulnerability that investors were beginning to price. Capital had poured into two large facilities — the Bethlehem, Pennsylvania campus and the Taunton, Somerset mega-facility completed in 2018 — in anticipation of compound annual growth rates premised on a VCSEL cycle that would sustain and broaden into automotive sensing, augmented reality and industrial applications. It did not broaden fast enough to compensate for what came next.

## Normalisation and the false dawn: 2021–2022

Fiscal year 2021 delivered the first sharp correction. Revenue fell to £154 million as Apple's VCSEL procurement moderated and the broader consumer electronics inventory cycle, supercharged by pandemic-era pull-forward demand, began its reversal. IQE's management characterised the environment with deliberate restraint, pointing to wireless and RF end-market strength and the early promise of photonics diversification, while acknowledging that headline momentum had stalled. The post-VCSEL normalisation, it was becoming clear, was structural.

The 2022 result — £167 million — appeared, on the surface, like a recovery. RF business serving 5G handset production and base station build-out provided a partial offset. But the year's more consequential development was a governance intervention: in February 2022, the board brought in Americo Lemos as Group Chief Executive, replacing the long-serving founder Drew Nelson. Lemos arrived from GlobalFoundries, where he had been Senior Vice President of Manufacturing — a background that signalled the board's diagnosis that IQE's primary challenge was operational rather than strategic: facility utilisation, cost structure, and manufacturing execution. He was an industrialist rather than a compound semiconductor technologist in the traditional IQE mould, and his public statements emphasised efficiency, capital discipline, and customer intimacy. He inherited a company carrying the cost base of two large, under-utilised facilities and a revenue line that had retreated from its peak.

## The trough: 2023 and the £115 million reckoning

If 2022 offered false optimism, 2023 delivered a definitive reckoning. Full-year revenue contracted to £115.3 million — the lowest since the early years of the VCSEL build-up, and a level that rendered the fixed-cost infrastructure inherited from the expansion years acutely painful. Gross margins compressed under the weight of idle capacity, and the adjusted operating loss reflected not merely market softness but a structural mismatch between asset base and recoverable demand.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (£m) | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 140.0 | VCSEL ramp; RF strength |
| 2020 | 178.0 | Apple VCSEL volume peak |
| 2021 | 154.0 | Post-peak normalisation begins |
| 2022 | 167.0 | RF partial offset; Lemos appointed |
| 2023 | 115.3 | Post-VCSEL trough; facilities underutilised |

The causes were multiple and reinforcing. The smartphone RF cycle weakened as Chinese handset OEMs drew down inventory rather than placing fresh epiwafer orders. VCSEL demand for consumer sensing showed no recovery. Photonics for datacom — the category that would eventually anchor the InP recovery narrative — remained too small to offset losses elsewhere. The Bethlehem facility, constructed to serve a compound semiconductor market still largely anticipated rather than present, carried fixed costs at utilisation rates that management acknowledged were unsustainable.

Lemos and his team held to a consistent strategic argument throughout the year: the infrastructure had been built for markets — InP photonics for AI datacentre interconnect, power electronics for electrification, next-generation RF front-end — that were arriving, but on timelines that were frustrating capital markets expectations. The message was disciplined and, to analysts who had heard variants of it since 2019, increasingly difficult to credit against the reported numbers.

IQE's equity told the story management could not rewrite. Shares that had touched 170 pence on AIM during the 2017-2018 VCSEL mania had compressed into single-digit pence territory by late 2023, valuing the company at a fraction of its replacement-cost infrastructure. Institutional holders reduced positions, and the debate circulating among compound semiconductor investors was whether the pure-play epitaxy foundry model could sustain the capital intensity its ambitions required.

## October 2024: Lemos departs, the board resets

In October 2024, after two and a half years in post, Americo Lemos stepped down as Chief Executive. The board announced the transition without a simultaneous permanent appointment — a sequencing that investors read as an indication of urgency. Chris Meadows, in the non-executive chair capacity, provided immediate continuity alongside CFO Jutta Meier, whose tenure across multiple CEO transitions had made her the institutional memory of IQE's financial architecture and the constant in each leadership renegotiation.

The Lemos era had not been without progress. The company had continued to serve its blue-chip customer base — Lumentum, Coherent (formerly II-VI), Broadcom and WIN Semiconductors among them — and had maintained its position as the go-to independent epitaxy supplier for technically demanding applications. Restructuring actions had moderated the cost base. But the revenue trajectory had not recovered toward 2020 or even 2022 levels, and the facilities overhang remained unresolved. The board's decision reflected, in the characteristically understated language of AIM RNS announcements, a judgement that the pace of operational execution needed acceleration.

## 2025 and the InP inflection thesis

The appointment of Steve Smith as permanent Group Chief Executive in 2025 framed a new strategic posture. Smith entered a business where the macro demand environment had shifted materially from the 2023 trough conditions. The AI infrastructure build-out — hyperscale data centres deploying 800G and 1.6T optical transceiver technology at scale — had begun to generate measurable pull on InP epiwafer demand, and IQE, with established InP epitaxy capability and available capacity at Bethlehem, was positioned to benefit from the inflection.

The photonics thesis rested on the semiconductor physics of high-bandwidth optical interconnect. Each 800G transceiver consumed multiple InP-based components — distributed feedback laser chips, electro-absorption modulators, photodetectors — whose performance specifications demanded precisely controlled indium phosphide epitaxy of the kind IQE had spent years qualifying at tier-1 transceiver manufacturers. As hyperscale capex accelerated through 2024 and into 2025, lead-time signals from the transceiver supply chain tightened, and IQE's customer conversations were reported to have shifted from qualification programmes toward volume discussions.

Smith's public communications emphasised operational restructuring: driving Bethlehem toward productive utilisation thresholds, rationalising the cost base to near-term revenue realities, and investing in the InP qualification pipeline. The narrative arc from the 2023 trough toward a recovery built on AI photonics and RF cycle normalisation was the equity story management was constructing.

## Equity positioning and the test ahead

By the snapshot date of May 2026, IQE's shares remained at levels implying a substantial discount to the replacement cost of the installed reactor base. The distance between the 2017-2018 speculative peak — briefly above 170 pence, implying a market capitalisation approaching £1.3 billion — and the prevailing price reflected five years of compounding disappointment: the VCSEL unwind, the 2023 revenue collapse, the CEO transition, and persistent operating losses through the under-utilisation cycle.

The 2025 half-year results and the anticipated 2026 half-year report carried disproportionate weight as the first rigorous tests of whether InP volume was materialising fast enough to drive operating leverage through the fixed-cost base. The analyst community, cautious after years of missed recovery calls, was watching utilisation rates and gross margin progression as the leading indicators of whether the InP inflection had crossed from strategic narrative into reported numbers. The underlying question — not whether compound semiconductor epitaxy mattered to AI photonics infrastructure, which it plainly did, but whether IQE's balance sheet and management could capture the cycle before capital markets demanded a renegotiation of terms — was the one framing every investor conversation as the company entered the second half of the decade.

chapters.title: Steve Smith (CEO), Jutta Meier, and the Non-Executive Chair
chapters.body:
The boardroom rupture that reshaped IQE plc's leadership arrived without ceremony. On 29 October 2024, the Cardiff-based compound semiconductor maker filed a brief RNS announcement stating that Americo Lemos had left the role of Chief Executive Officer with immediate effect. [The disclosure](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/iqe-announces-departure-of-chief-executive-officer/) ran to fewer than two hundred words and offered no rationale. Within hours, the company had elevated its recently arrived Chief Financial Officer, Jutta Meier, to an interim dual role while simultaneously installing the incoming Chairman, Mark Cubitt, as Executive Chair — a structure that would persist, in modified form, until IQE's full-year 2024 results the following May confirmed Meier as permanent chief executive.

## The Lemos Era: January 2022 – October 2024

Americo Lemos arrived at IQE with a CV shaped by the global semiconductor supply chain's biggest names. [Announced on 22 November 2021](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2021/11/22/2338630/0/en/IQE-plc-Leadership-Announcement-Americo-Lemos-appointed-as-ceo-of-iqe.html) and taking office on 10 January 2022, he succeeded IQE's founder Dr. Drew Nelson after a deliberate external search. His most recent role had been Senior Vice President of Business Development for Asia Pacific and China Country President at GlobalFoundries Inc., adding to prior executive positions at Qualcomm, Intel, Flextronics, Texas Instruments, and Skyworks. The breadth of that pedigree — spanning fabless customer development, advanced wafer foundry, and electronics manufacturing — made him an unusual fit for a specialist compound semiconductor epitaxy house. Then-Chairman Phil Smith framed the appointment in expansive terms:

> "Americo is the ideal leader to take over from IQE's founder Dr Drew Nelson, who I would like to thank for his years of passion."

The £200,000 share award granted on joining, subject to a three-year clawback, signalled alignment expectations. Lemos inherited a business in cyclical difficulty. The Apple VCSEL demand surge that had powered IQE's photonics revenues through 2021 unwound sharply as Face ID adoption plateaued and Apple diversified its VCSEL sourcing. Wireless revenues, meanwhile, were caught between handset OEM inventory destocking and a slower-than-forecast 5G infrastructure build-out. IQE's revenue dropped to £113.1m in its 2023 financial year — a 31 per cent decline from the prior year's £164.4m — with adjusted EBITDA collapsing from £25.7m to £4.3m. Whether the board's October 2024 decision to part ways with Lemos after 33 months reflected a strategic disagreement over capital allocation, footprint rationalisation timing, or the pace of cost restructuring was never publicly explained. What the company communicated was that Cubitt and Meier would together "execute on the near-term pipeline" and drive "cash generation across the Group" — language signalling that balance-sheet discipline had moved firmly to the centre of IQE's immediate agenda.

## Jutta Meier: From Intel Foundry to Chief Executive

Jutta Meier, aged 57 at the time of her [CFO appointment](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/appointment-of-jutta-meier-as-chief-financial-officer/) on 22 January 2024, arrived at IQE from Intel Corporation, where she had been Senior Finance Director at Intel Foundry Services — Intel's capital-intensive foundry transformation business. Before Intel she had served as Vice President of Finance at GlobalFoundries Inc., and in various senior finance roles at Advanced Micro Devices Inc., accumulating more than 25 years of continuous experience across the compound semiconductor and advanced logic sectors. That career arc — AMD, GlobalFoundries, Intel Foundry Services — placed her at the precise intersection of manufacturing-scale finance and process-technology transformation that IQE's board needed.

Lemos, in welcoming her to the CFO seat, framed the hire in operational terms:

> "Her skills and experience gained within global semiconductor manufacturing will be an important asset to IQE, enabling her to drive value creation and improve margins."

Meier had been in post for barely nine months when Lemos departed. She stepped into the interim CEO role while retaining the CFO portfolio — an unusual dual burden she carried without a formal title split for the following six months. At the full-year 2024 results on 13 May 2025, the board formalised what the market had broadly already concluded: Meier would become IQE's permanent Chief Executive, continuing to hold both portfolios. The company noted female representation on the board had reached 57 per cent.

Her own framing of the stabilisation effort was direct:

> "IQE delivered a solid set of financials in line with our January 2025 trading update. Our focus has been on reducing costs and optimising our footprint."

The [2024 results](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2025/full-year-2024-results/) showed genuine operational progress: adjusted EBITDA recovered to £8.1m, up 88 per cent from £4.3m, on revenues of £118.0m — essentially flat year-on-year but against a sharply improved cost structure. Wireless revenue grew 25 per cent to £67.3m; photonics revenue fell 16 per cent to £49.9m, still absorbing the VCSEL inventory correction. Headcount reductions of more than 10 per cent and SG&A cuts of 8 per cent underlined that her mandate was as much about cost architecture as revenue growth. A comprehensive Strategic Review — encompassing a potential full sale of IQE Taiwan alongside a possible IPO of that subsidiary — was under way at the snapshot date.

## Mark Cubitt: Executive Chair

Mark Cubitt joined IQE's board on 8 October 2024 as an independent non-executive director and Chair-elect, [appointed](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2024/appointment-of-non-executive-director-and-chair-elect/) to succeed Phil Smith, who had served on the board for nearly nine years — five of them as Chairman. Smith departed effective 1 January 2025, ending one of the longer non-executive tenures at an AIM-listed technology company.

Cubitt, aged 61 at appointment, brought semiconductor pedigree through the back office. He had spent more than seven years as Chief Financial Officer at Wolfson Microelectronics plc, the Edinburgh-based audio semiconductor group, through its acquisition by Cirrus Logic in August 2014 — one of the more consequential AIM semiconductor exits of that decade. That experience gave him direct familiarity with the customer concentration dynamics and M&A pressures that characterise compound and mixed-signal semiconductor businesses. He had since built a portfolio of non-executive chairmanships, holding concurrent positions at Concurrent Technologies plc (embedded processor solutions) and Beeks Financial Cloud Group plc (capital markets cloud infrastructure), and had earlier chaired Superglass Holdings plc through a turnaround before its eventual sale. Phil Smith's valedictory observation at the Cubitt appointment was pointed:

> "Mark brings a wealth of expertise to the Company, with a deep knowledge of the technology sector and significant Board-level experience."

When Meier was confirmed as permanent CEO in May 2025, Cubitt contextualised what her six-month dual role had accomplished:

> "Jutta has stabilised and refocused the business and rebuilt confidence with both customers and employees since taking the interim role."

## The Non-Executive Bench

By the frozen snapshot date, IQE's non-executive board comprised five directors whose combined backgrounds spanned the full semiconductor supply chain from foundry to fabless customer.

**Carol Chesney** served as Senior Independent Director and chaired the Audit & Risk Committee, sitting also on the Remuneration and Nominations Committees. She joined the IQE board in May 2019 and was confirmed as SID in November 2020. A career that began at Arthur Andersen led to her Fellowship of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales. At the snapshot date she simultaneously chaired the audit committees of Renishaw plc (a role held continuously since October 2012), Imagination Technologies, Hunting plc, and Biffa plc — a depth of concurrent audit committee responsibility unusual even by the standards of experienced independent directors in UK technology and industrials.

**Victoria Hull** joined IQE effective 1 August 2021 and chaired the Remuneration Committee, also sitting on the Audit & Risk and Nominations Committees as one of the two designated board workforce representatives. [Her appointment](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2021/07/29/2270896/0/en/IQE-plc-Appointment-of-Victoria-Hull-as-Non-Executive-Director.html) followed a career that began as a trainee solicitor at Clifford Chance LLP before she moved to an executive directorship at Invensys — the industrial technology group subsequently absorbed by Schneider Electric — providing hands-on experience of complex multi-geography manufacturing operations. She subsequently built a portfolio across Alphawave IP Group plc, Network International Holdings plc, and Ultra Electronics Holdings plc, where she served as Senior Independent Director.

**Maria Marced** — formally Dr. Maria Angeles Marced Martin — joined effective 1 January 2024, one of [two new non-executive directors](https://www.iqep.com/media/press-releases/2023/iqe-board-appointments/) announced on 29 November 2023. She brought arguably the most directly relevant semiconductor pedigree on the NED bench: President of TSMC Europe for more than 16 years, preceded by Senior Vice President roles at NXP Semiconductors and 19 years as Vice President and EMEA General Manager at Intel Corporation. She holds a PhD in Telecommunications Engineering from the Polytechnic University of Madrid. Her membership of the Remuneration and ESG Committees brought IQE's governance a line of sight into the supply-chain dynamics and capacity planning priorities of the foundry ecosystem within which IQE's customers operate.

**Bami Bastani** — Dr. Bamdad Bastani, aged 70 at appointment — joined simultaneously with Marced from 1 January 2024. He brought seven years at GlobalFoundries in successively senior roles: first as Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Mobile and Wireless Infrastructure Business Unit, then as Senior Vice President and Senior Advisor to the CEO. Before GlobalFoundries he had held President and CEO roles at Meru Networks, Trident Microsystems, and ANADIGICS, and sat on the Global Semiconductor Alliance board for seven years. His committee assignments — Audit & Risk and ESG, with a board workforce representative designation — placed him at the governance intersection of financial controls and operational sustainability in the RF semiconductor space most relevant to IQE's wireless business.

**Harmesh Suniara** joined on 30 June 2023 as the designated representative of Lombard Odier 1798 Volantis, which at the time of his appointment held approximately 141.6 million ordinary shares representing around 14.7 per cent of IQE's issued share capital — the company's largest single disclosed shareholder. Aged 52, Suniara brought more than 15 years of investment management experience focused on UK small and mid-cap equities with a particular emphasis on technology and life sciences. He also served as a non-executive director at Actual Experience plc. His presence on the board formalised Lombard Odier's capacity to engage directly with IQE's strategy as the company worked through its restructuring and footprint rationalisation cycle.

## Governance Architecture

IQE operates under the UK Corporate Governance Code as adapted for AIM-listed companies — a framework that permits a smaller executive leadership team relative to a Main Market listing while still requiring a majority of independent non-executive directors and clearly delineated Audit, Remuneration, and Nominations Committees. The dual CEO and CFO role held by Meier at the snapshot date was presented in the context of the post-Lemos stabilisation period rather than as a permanent structural choice, though no timetable for separating the portfolios had been publicly announced. With female directors at 57 per cent of board composition and a NED cohort whose executive experience collectively spanned TSMC, GlobalFoundries, Intel, Wolfson Microelectronics, and Invensys, the governance structure assembled around Meier's leadership provided a depth of compound semiconductor and capital-markets expertise that its AIM peer group would have found difficult to match.
